origin.namedBy: Pieter Dirkszoon Keyser and Frederick de Houtman; first shown by Petrus Plancius
history: Chamaeleon is one of the twelve southern constellations formed from the observations of the Dutch navigators Pieter Dirkszoon Keyser and Frederick de Houtman, who charted the far-southern sky in 1595–97 on the first Dutch voyage to the East Indies. Petrus Plancius first drew the new figures on a celestial globe in 1598, and other mapmakers, including Johann Bayer in his 1603 atlas *Uranometria*, adopted them quickly because no other measurements of those stars existed.

The fleet spent months in 1595 resting at Madagascar, where chameleons are common. One of the expedition's chroniclers, Willem Lodewyckz, recorded watching them shoot out their tongues to catch flies. That is why the sky has a chameleon with a fly, Musca, right beside it. On Plancius's first globe the fly sits unnamed above the lizard's head; in 1600 the globe maker Jodocus Hondius redrew the pair so the chameleon is flicking its tongue at the insect.

Early charts drew the animal with its feet toward the south celestial pole. Edmond Halley turned it over on his southern chart of 1678 so that its back is to the pole, and it has been drawn that way since. There is no myth attached to it.

overview: Chamaeleon is the color-changing lizard seen by Dutch sailors in Madagascar: a small, dim diamond of 4th-magnitude stars only about ten degrees from the south celestial pole.
howToFind: Chamaeleon never rises from mid-northern latitudes. Its main stars only clear the horizon south of about latitude 10°N, and it is best from the Southern Hemisphere, where it circles the pole and is in the sky every night of the year.

Use the [[asterism:southern-cross|Southern Cross]]. Follow the long bar of the Cross from [[star:Gacrux|Gacrux]] at the top through [[star:Acrux|Acrux]] at the foot and keep going toward the pole. A little under two fists beyond Acrux, and slightly west of that line, you reach [[star:γ Cha|Gamma Chamaeleontis]] in the middle of the constellation. Another route: from [[star:Miaplacidus|Miaplacidus]], the bright star at the foot of Carina, [[star:α Cha|Alpha Chamaeleontis]] is less than a fist toward the pole.
shape: A stretched diamond of four faint stars more than a fist long, sometimes called the Frying Pan in Australia. All of them are near magnitude 4, so the figure disappears in a city sky and needs real darkness to stand out.

mainStars.note: Magnitude 4.1, a white star only about 64 light-years away, at the western end of the diamond.
Magnitude 4.1, a red giant about 420 light-years away; binoculars show its warm tint.
Magnitude 4.2, a blue-white star roughly 300 light-years away at the eastern end.
A wide double: a blue-white star of magnitude 4.4 with an orange companion of magnitude 5.5 nearby.

notableObjects.note: Delta-1 and Delta-2 Chamaeleontis make an easy binocular pair with contrasting orange and blue-white colors.
A faint planetary nebula (the puffed-off shell of a dying star). In a telescope it is a small gray disk about the apparent size of Jupiter.

facts: The chameleon and the fly are a matched pair: sailors on the first Dutch voyage to the East Indies watched chameleons catching flies on Madagascar.
Dark clouds of dust in Chamaeleon, a few hundred light-years away, are among the nearest places where new low-mass stars are forming.
